design_detail: Narrative review comparing cannabis flower, concentrates and edibles on prevalence of use (mainly US samples), methods of consumption and cannabis use disorder (CUD) outcomes. PubMed keyword searches screened for relevance by title and abstract, plus backward and forward citation searches; 27 articles included (Figure 1), 72 references listed. No eligibility criteria beyond relevance, no search dates, no appraisal of the included studies; the authors scored their own review 12 of 12 on SANRA, a scale for the quality of narrative reviews. Published online 26 October 2024; issue dated 2026.
can_establish: What a 2024 narrative reading of mostly US survey studies says about which forms of cannabis people use and about CUD by form, and which comparisons the authors found missing (form-specific longitudinal data, CUD with edibles, flower by mode of use).
cannot_establish: Whether concentrates, flower or edibles differ in CUD risk, or by how much: there is no systematic search, no appraisal and no pooling, and the CUD evidence it cites is cross-sectional.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). PubMed searches combining 'cannabis' with a form, a method of consumption or CUD terms; studies kept if the title or abstract mentioned both the form and the outcome or method; further studies from reference lists and PubMed's Cited By feature (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 4; Figure 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Relevance to a form of cannabis and its prevalence, method of consumption or CUD outcomes; 3,861 articles excluded on title or abstract and 196 at relevance review (Figure 1). No dates, languages, designs or quality thresholds are stated, and who screened is not stated.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. The cited samples are mostly from the US: national adult surveys, college students, high-school students in Colorado and Los Angeles, web-based and Twitter-based samples of people who use concentrates, and medical cannabis patients.
sample.selection_effects: One database and no stated search dates. The reference list does not include the 2022 systematic review of potency and mental ill health and addiction (Petrilli et al., 2022) or the UK and multinational survey studies of potency and dependence that it covers (editors' check of the 72 references). The prevalence part is restricted to US samples by design; the CUD part draws on US college, high-school, web and national samples.

exposure.measurement: As in the cited studies: self-reported form and frequency of use in surveys; no measured THC.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Forms as the authors define them: flower (raw plant material), concentrates (material extracted from the plant to increase potency; typically about three times the THC content of flower or more, as cited), and edibles (products for oral ingestion). Product content as cited only.
exposure.polysubstance: Blunts (cannabis rolled in a tobacco wrap) are flagged as a confounder of flower findings because they add tobacco; otherwise not addressed.

comparison.controls: Comparisons across forms within the cited surveys (frequent concentrate use against frequent flower use or no concentrate use; one form against several; inhaled forms against edibles); none with people who do not use cannabis.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed. The authors note that people who frequently use concentrates may also use higher-potency cannabis when not using concentrates, and that frequency of use is the most reliable predictor of CUD across forms, both of which bear on any comparison by form.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed except tobacco in blunts.

outcomes.instruments: As in the cited studies (CUD symptom counts and severity, problematic use, tolerance and withdrawal, worry about one's use); the review does not name the instruments.
outcomes.validity_norms: No appraisal of the cited studies; the SANRA score is the authors' own rating of their review.
outcomes.operationalization: CUD outcomes are described as types such as symptom count, severity and problematic use (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 5).

analysis.effect_sizes: None for CUD comparisons. Prevalence percentages are reported as cited, for example US adults in 2017 (n = 9,003): past-year flower smoking 12.9%, vaporizing 4.7%, concentrates 1.9% and edibles 6%.
analysis.selective_reporting: Null findings on concentrates and CUD reported elsewhere (a US sample of 156 in the 2022 systematic review) are not cited; the cited survey of 191 people is described as showing heightened CUD symptoms with frequent concentrate use, a difference the 2022 systematic review reports as not statistically significant.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The CUD evidence by form that the review cites is a handful of cross-sectional US surveys: one of 191 people comparing frequent concentrate with frequent flower use (Bidwell et al., 2018), surveys of dab or butane hash oil use in web and college samples (Sagar et al., 2018; Meier, 2017), surveys linking more frequent use of the inhaled forms but not edibles to problematic use (Steeger et al., 2021) and high-frequency use of all three forms to more CUD than high-frequency flower-only use (Gunn et al., 2020), a college survey linking flower potency to CUD symptom count (Piercey et al., 2024), and a US study linking average potency to a first CUD symptom (Arterberry et al., 2019). For edibles it finds no CUD data and argues by analogy from studies of slower-acting formulations of other drugs. It finds no form-specific longitudinal data.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Results state that concentrate use has consistently been associated with increased CUD risk compared with other forms, and the Highlights state as a fact that concentrate use "is associated with more severe cannabis use disorder outcomes"; the Abstract says only that it may be. Gaps: (1) 'consistently' rests mainly on one cross-sectional survey of 191 people, which the 2022 systematic review reports as showing no significant difference between frequent concentrate and frequent herbal use (editors' comparison; the primary paper was not read), plus surveys that compare people by how often they use concentrates rather than by form; (2) the Discussion's own conclusions, that frequency of use is the most reliable predictor across forms and that causal roles of quantity and potency are not established, are not carried into the Highlights; (3) case reports of paranoia and psychosis-like symptoms after concentrate use are called alarming; (4) the 12 of 12 SANRA score, including for the literature search, is self-assigned. Against this, the Abstract and Conclusion say plainly that comparisons across forms are scarce and form-specific longitudinal data are lacking, and the edibles section says the CUD risk is unknown.

timeline.event: Bidwell et al. (2018), a US cross-sectional study of 191 people buying concentrates and flower on the legal market (doi 10.1016/j.abrep.2018.08.004), the main source of this review's statement on concentrates and CUD; not read here.
Meta-analysis of the prevalence of cannabis use disorder among people who use cannabis (not cited by this review)
Systematic review of potency and mental ill health and addiction, which reports the same 191-person study as showing no significant difference (not cited by this review)

replication.where_it_stands: A narrative review that adds no new evidence on CUD by form. Its statement on concentrates traces mainly to one cross-sectional survey that the 2022 systematic review describes differently, and it omits that review. It is useful for the gaps it names (edibles, form-specific longitudinal data, mode of flower use) and for US prevalence figures as cited; claims should trace any CUD figure to the primary studies.

funding.funder: No funding associated with the preparation of the review (Funding, p. 10).
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest reported by the authors (Disclosure statement, p. 10).
funding.affiliations_note: Oregon State University (Department of Integrative Biology; School of Psychological Science). No study by the authors is among the cited sources for the CUD findings (editors' check of the reference list). No cannabis-industry or tobacco-industry ties are printed.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts of people who use cannabis that record each form used, its labelled or tested THC content, and how much and how often it is used, and that measure DSM-5 cannabis use disorder by interview over years, analysed with frequency and amount as possible confounders or mediators and including enough people who mainly use edibles.

domains.note: PubMed only, no dates, no eligibility criteria beyond relevance, screening by unstated reviewers; the main systematic review on potency and addiction (2022) and the survey studies it covers are missing from the 72 references.
No appraisal. Designs are sometimes named (survey, case reports), but no study's limits are weighed, and 'consistently' rests on one cross-sectional study.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: No study by the authors is cited for the review's findings (editors' check of the reference list).

Hedged in the Abstract and Conclusions ('may', 'suggest'), but the Highlights state the concentrate association without a hedge, and the edibles argument by analogy from formulations of other drugs sits beside the data.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a higher CUD risk with concentrates (evidence of no difference under-represented)
domains.note: A null comparison of concentrates with herbal cannabis (US sample of 156) is not cited, and the cited 191-person survey's non-significant difference is presented as heightened symptoms; the review does note that frequency predicts CUD across forms and that potency's causal role is not established.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The selection is unsystematic and misses the main systematic review, the cited studies are not appraised, and the concentrate statement in the Results and Highlights is stronger than its main cross-sectional source; on the other hand the review is explicit that comparisons by form and longitudinal data are lacking. It may be cited for what it says, for the gaps it names and for US prevalence figures as cited; its statement on concentrates and CUD should be traced to the primary studies, and it is not evidence of a CUD difference by form.

key_findings.finding: Methods: PubMed keyword searches screened for relevance by title and abstract; 4,077 articles found, 3,861 excluded, 216 reviewed for relevance, 196 excluded, 20 included, 7 added from reference lists and citing articles, 27 in the review. The authors rated their own review on SANRA and scored it 2 of 2 in all six areas (12 of 12).

Flower: among US adults (n = 9,003), 12.9% reported past-year flower smoking, more than edibles and concentrates combined; 94.6% of college-age people who used cannabis in the past year (n = 1,390) had ever used flower; among Colorado high-school students who currently used cannabis (n = 4,637), 76.1% had used flower in the past 30 days and 53.1% named it their usual form. Flower potency is cited as having risen from about 4% THC in 1995 to over 12% in 2014 and commonly 20% or more by 2020, with dispensary flower testing at 13% to 36%.

Concentrates: among US adults in 2017 (n = 9,003), 4.7% reported vaporizing cannabis, 1.9% concentrates and 6% edibles in the past year; 44.2% of the college-age sample had ever used concentrates; among the Colorado high-school students, 47.1% had used concentrates in the past 30 days and 17.4% named them their usual form (edibles 9.5%); in web-based studies with over 600 participants each, 13% of people who used concentrates did so daily or near daily. Concentrates are described as typically about three times the THC of flower or more, from 50-60% to over 90% THC, as cited. The authors note a lack of recent nationally representative data on concentrate use.

Edibles: 6% of US adults reported past-year edible use; among Los Angeles high-school students (n = 2,163), 17.5% had ever used edibles against 25.8% flower; among the Colorado high-school students, 34.3% had used edibles in the past 30 days and 9.5% named them their usual form.

Flower and CUD: a cross-sectional survey of Colorado college students (n = 617; ref. 36) found flower potency positively associated with CUD symptom count and severity; bong use (refs 18, 20-22) and blunt frequency (refs 26-28) are cited as associated with more frequent use, problematic symptoms, tolerance or CUD. The authors say the literature lacks CUD data for flower compared with other forms.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis flower › Methods of consumption, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 5); Results › Cannabis flower › CUD outcomes, paragraph (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Concentrates and CUD: the review states that concentrate use has consistently been associated with higher CUD risk than other forms; that people who frequently use concentrates show more CUD symptoms than people who do not use them but may also use higher-potency cannabis when not using concentrates, and report fewer positive effects from concentrates (ref. 40, Bidwell et al., 2018); that people who use concentrates chronically may show more tolerance and withdrawal (ref. 37, a 2021 review); that people who regularly use concentrates more often feel worried about their use than people who have tried them (ref. 42, a national web survey of dab use); and that among college students more frequent use of butane hash oil went with more physical symptoms such as tolerance after adjustment for demographic, substance-use and personality covariates (ref. 43). Longitudinal studies of long-term concentrate use are called for. No effect sizes are given.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis concentrates › CUD outcomes, paragraph; references 37, 40, 42 and 43 (p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Edibles and CUD: there is limited information specific to the CUD potential of edibles. The review argues from studies of other drugs (refs 50 and 51, on formulations of hydrocodone and methylphenidate) that a slower onset of action goes with a lower potential to contribute to a substance use disorder, and cites one source (ref. 44, titled as a study of medical cannabis patients with chronic pain) for people who use cannabis medically preferring oral use and for people new to non-medical use or using it infrequently more often naming edibles as their primary form. The section concludes that the CUD outcomes of edibles have not been sufficiently characterised.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cannabis edibles › CUD outcomes, paragraph; Results › Cannabis edibles › Conclusion, paragraph

key_findings.finding: Across forms, the Discussion describes the literature on problematic use as small and incomplete and mostly about flower. It cites a positive association between product potency and CUD risk (ref. 52), more CUD symptoms with frequent concentrate use than with frequent flower use (ref. 40), more problematic use with more frequent use of the two inhaled forms but not edibles (ref. 39), and more CUD with high-frequency use of all three forms than with high-frequency flower-only use (ref. 15); it states, without a citation, that inhalation is generally associated with a higher CUD risk than ingestion. It concludes that frequency of use remains the most reliable predictor of CUD risk across all forms and that further causal factors, such as quantity and THC potency, have yet to be firmly established.

Other harms, as cited: smoking flower linked to asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease but not reported as a significant contributor to lung cancer or irreversible airway changes (refs 54-58); case reports of paranoia and psychosis-like symptoms after concentrate use (refs 62-64); edibles commonly associated with hospital visits for accidental ingestion or over-intoxication (ref. 65), while in a survey of 172 people who had an uncomfortable experience with edibles, 95.2% reported no medical problem from it (ref. 66).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Other acute and chronic health complications, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Abstract and Highlights: concentrate use may be associated with a greater CUD risk (Abstract); concentrate use is associated with more severe CUD outcomes, and edible CUD risk is unclear (Highlights). Conclusion: few single studies report all three forms, and form-specific long-term data are lacking.
No funding; no potential conflict of interest reported.

reporting_issues.issue: A sentence on dry herb vaping is garbled as printed: after lower plasma carbon monoxide, the next sentence reads as a fragment comparing respiratory toxicity with flower smoke at comparable plasma THC, so what ref. 30 found cannot be told from the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The basis of the review's suggestion that dry herb vaping may be a safer alternative for people who use cannabis chronically cannot be checked from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Ref. 44, titled as a cross-sectional study of medical cannabis patients with chronic pain, is cited for statements about non-medical use (people new to it or using it infrequently naming edibles as their main form; flower and concentrates being more popular among people who use cannabis non-medically) and for vaporization having risen to a prevalence comparable to smoking.
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements may not rest on samples of non-medical use; the primary paper was not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says 44.2% of the college-age sample had ever used concentrates, which is only 20% less than the number who had ever used edibles, without giving the edible figure for that sample.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the gap is relative or in percentage points cannot be told.

reporting_issues.issue: The same 191-person survey (Bidwell et al., 2018) is described here as showing heightened CUD symptoms in people who frequently use concentrates, while the 2022 systematic review reports no significant difference (means 2.1 and 1.3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's main source for concentrates and CUD is reported differently by two reviews; the primary paper (doi 10.1016/j.abrep.2018.08.004) should be read before either description is used.
